title: Priority inversion in MoE commit paths: latency sources & mitigation playbook
content:
Purpose:
This note collects experiments and tracing that point to a priority-inversion style phenomenon in our MoE commit/serialize paths that is producing sporadic 95/99 tail latency spikes for long-context Llama/Mistral sessions. It focuses on root causes visible in the request commit path (GPU handoff, per-session serialization, and CPU-side locks) and proposes a short-to-medium term mitigation playbook.

Background / why I care:
- Multiple customer incidents in Jan–Feb 2025 showed 99th token latency > 3x baseline for requests that had a mix of small and large tokens and where routing selected 1–3 hot experts.
- These spikes are not explained by GPU memory pressure or PCIe faults (those were separate investigations). Instead, traces show single long-running enqueue/commit operations blocking higher-priority token emissions from other sessions on the same worker.

Symptoms observed (telemetry highlights):
- 95/99 latency correlated with commit_duration_ms on worker X (trace ID samples: XTR-20250211-9f3a, XTR-20250214-21b7).
- CPU-side mutex hold times spike concurrently with GPU stream synchronize calls (cpu_mutex_hold_ms increases when commit_duration_ms > 30ms).
- Tail spikes disproportionately affect sessions with long-context and alternating bursts (chat style: user message then model context flush).
- Hot experts amplify the effect: when expert fanout > 8 and expert selection skew > 0.6, probability of tail event increases ~2.7x (from batch telemetry summary).

Trace excerpt (summary):
- Request A (high-priority interactive): arrives and is ready to emit tokens, acquires session serialization lock but blocks on global commit queue because Request B (large background request) is in the middle of committing large per-expert activation blobs to GPU and performing a blocking stream sync.
- Timeline: Request B enters commit -> copies NVMM->GPU for several experts -> issues cudaStreamSynchronize (blocking) while holding the scheduler spinlock -> Request A waits on the scheduler lock => visible as priority inversion in traces.

Microbench notes (local repro attempts):
- Repro harness: moe_commit_stress.py (local) that issues synthetic sessions with controllable expert fanout, activation size, and interleaving priority flags.
- Baseline: single session commit cost ~8–12ms. Interleaved case (high fanout + concurrent small sessions) produced observed blocking where the concurrent small session experienced commit-wait of 35–120ms depending on GPU/PCIe.
- Disabling stream-level synchronize and switching to event-based poll reduced observed blocking by ~60% in the harness.

Hypotheses (ordered):
1) Global commit ordering + blocking CUDA synchronizes cause CPU-side lock hold while GPU stream drains; high-latency commit ops block unrelated sessions (classic priority inversion).
2) Our per-worker scheduler uses a single global serialization lock for commit ordering; the lock is coarse-grained and held during both memory copies and stream sync.
3) Hot-expert memory copy patterns create long-duration CUDA ops that are more likely to trigger the inversion when concurrent interactive sessions exist.
4) Kernel preemption is not available (or not used) so long CUDA ops cannot be interrupted to let smaller critical operations proceed.

Experiment matrix and results (short):
- E1: Replace streamSync with event-poll loop (non-blocking): reduces tail by ~50–70% in harness; small increase in CPU polling cost.
- E2: Move memory copies off critical commit lock (copy under per-expert buffer lock, release global commit lock early): reduces mutex hold time, tail reduction ~40%.
- E3: Introduce priority-aware queue where sessions tagged interactive are allowed to cut in front of background commits (preempt commit if safe): prototype reduced interactive tail to baseline but introduced additional complexity and rare consistency races in KV cache state (needs careful handshake).

Risks and constraints:
- Preempting commits may violate ordering assumptions in current commit protocol (we rely on commit ordering for deterministic KV cache state). Must prove linearizability after preemption.
- Event-poll approach increases CPU usage; need to quantify cost at scale (CPU credits on Dedicated nodes).
- Changing lock granularity may reveal other races (we saw an allocation double-free in one early experiment — fixed by adding a small refcount guard).

Short-term mitigations (safe, low-risk):
- Disable cudaStreamSynchronize in the hot path and replace with cudaEventQuery-based polling where possible (feature flag gated). Owner: Samir. Timeline: 1 week for canary on dev cluster.
- Reduce commit critical section to only metadata updates; move large memcopies to per-expert buffer stage before acquiring global commit lock. Owner: Ethan. Timeline: 2 weeks dev->staging.
- Add a tracing metric commit_lock_hold_ms (fine-grained) to detect regressions and alert when >10ms per-request. Owner: Priya. Timeline: 3 days.

Medium-term mitigations (higher effort):
- Implement priority-aware commit queue with safe preemption handshakes: requires KV-cache checkpointing around preemption points to ensure no partial state visible to other sessions. Design doc required. Owner: Marina. Timeline: 6–8 weeks.
- Rethink per-worker locking: move to per-expert or per-shard commit sequencing and use a re-order buffer to reconstruct global ordering only at emission time. This reduces contention but increases complexity for serialization and replay.

Long-term / architectural options:
- Explore GPU kernel preemption/ML-specific preempt hooks or smaller chunked kernels for very large activation blobs so long CUDA ops can be subdivided.
- Consider hybrid approach: small interactive sessions routed to a low-latency worker pool with stricter SLOs to avoid interference with batchy/large MoE commits. (This is similar to our selective routing ideas but focused on commit interference).

Playbook for oncall (quick):
1) If 95/99 spikes coincide with commit_lock_hold_ms > 20ms -> flip feature flag disable-stream-sync on worker pool for immediate mitigation.
2) If spikes continue, identify skewed expert usage via routing telemetry and add temporary routing cap for hot experts on affected workers (per-route emergency throttle).
3) Escalate to eng-serving-runtime with trace IDs and sample console live profile (run moe_commit_stress on worker).

Open questions / next experiments:
- How does the event-poll approach impact CPU utilization on Dedicated nodes under real mixed workloads? (run a week-long soak on staging with production-like mix)
- Are there correctness edge cases for preemptive commit when the routing layer replays session fragments? Need formal spec of KV-cache invariants to prove safe preemption.
- Can we detect hot-expert patterns early and proactively route to specialized queues before commit occurs? (cheap heuristic: short-term count per-session expert_skew metric).

Immediate next steps (owner list):
- Priya: add commit_lock_hold_ms metric, wire to console dashboard and alert (3d)
- Ethan: prototype reduced critical section and push to staging (2w)
- Samir: implement event-based stream polling in a feature-flagged branch and run harness (1w)
- Marina: draft priority-aware queue design doc and list invariants that must hold for KV cache (1 sprint)

Notes / misc:
- Repro harness, traces and helper scripts are in the linked PR + a local folder: tools/moe_commit_harness. See PR 1128 for initial event-poll patch.
- Observed that Llama and Mistral behave similarly; Qwen appears slightly more tolerant due to smaller activation per-expert in our builds (but needs dedicated check).

If you want to run the harness locally:
- python tools/moe_commit_harness/run.py --mode interleaved --fanout 8 --activation-size 32MB --threads 16
- Look at traces in /var/log/serving/traces/XTR-* and open mochatrace with sample id.

Tagged owners for sign-off: @samir @ethan @marina

-- end of note --
